name: Capacitors
description: Starting and running components with the right rating.
long_description: Capacitors give compressors and fan motors the extra push they need to start and stay running. They are one of the most common failure points in hot weather, and a correctly rated replacement (µF and voltage) is often a quick, low-cost fix.

parts.name: Compressor run capacitors
parts.detail: Keep the compressor running efficiently once started.
parts.summary: Run capacitors stay in circuit while the compressor runs, giving its motor the phase shift it needs to start and run efficiently. A weak capacitor causes hard starting, high current and overheating.
specs: Common AC values 20–60 µF; others to order
440/450 V AC (370 V AC on some units)
notes: Replace with the same µF value; the voltage can be the same or higher, never lower
Discharge the old capacitor before handling it

parts.name: Fan motor capacitors
parts.detail: For indoor blower and outdoor condenser fan motors.
parts.summary: Small run capacitors for indoor blower and outdoor condenser fan motors. A failed fan capacitor is a common reason for a fan that hums, runs slowly or only starts after a push.
specs: Indoor fans usually 1–3 µF; outdoor fans 2–10 µF
Rectangular plastic box or small round can
notes: Match the µF value printed on the old capacitor or the motor nameplate

parts.name: Dual-run capacitors
parts.detail: One unit serving both compressor and fan.
parts.summary: A dual-run capacitor combines the compressor and fan capacitors in one can, with a shared common terminal. They are common in outdoor units and window ACs.
specs: Metallised polypropylene film, two sections in one can
Compressor section 20–60 µF + fan section 2–10 µF (e.g. 35 + 5 µF)
notes: Both sections must match the original values
Mark the wires before removing the old capacitor so they go back on the right terminals

parts.name: Start capacitors & relays
parts.detail: Extra starting torque for hard-starting compressors.
parts.summary: Start capacitors give a compressor extra torque for the first moment of starting, then a relay or PTC starter takes them out of circuit. They help compressors that struggle to start under load or on low voltage.
specs: Rated as a range, e.g. 88–108 µF or 189–227 µF
A few seconds per start; not for continuous use
Potential (voltage) relays, current relays and PTC starters
Capacitor and relay combined, for single-phase compressors
notes: A start capacitor left in circuit will overheat and fail: check the relay too
Match the relay type and pick-up voltage to the compressor

signs: Fan spins slowly or needs a push
